overview.label: What you will learn
overview.value: How to decide whether a computer action is Safe to try, Ask first or Stop; how to judge whether an action is reversible; how to use fictional practice information; how to use Undo and Redo; and how to describe an unexpected result accurately.

overview.label: Why this matters at work
overview.value: Confidence does not mean clicking without concern. It means using a reliable process, recognising risk and knowing what to do when the screen behaves differently from expected.

overview.label: What you will produce
overview.value: A completed Safe Action Decision Record, an Undo and Redo practical record, an Unexpected Result Report, an open-book assessment and a personal Safe Action Quick Reference.

introduction.text: Circle or tick the number that best describes how confident you feel now. This is not a test and is not marked right or wrong.

introduction.label: The aim of this module
introduction.text: You are not expected to know every button or predict every problem. You are learning a process that lets you pause, classify an action, make a controlled change and explain what happened. That is practical digital confidence.

lesson.text: 2. Complete lesson
Read this section before completing any activity. Every decision rule, practical method and assessment answer appears here.
2.1 Digital confidence is a process

Digital confidence means being able to take a sensible next step, not knowing everything. A confident person can still pause, ask for approval or stop. What matters is making the decision calmly using what the screen actually shows.

At work, the safest approach is to separate low-impact practice from actions that affect real information, other people, accounts, money or security. This module uses three action categories so that you do not have to rely on guesswork.

lesson.label: Key idea
lesson.text: Pausing is not failure. Pausing gives you time to read the screen and choose the correct category.
2.2 The three action categories

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what the three action categories changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.

rows: A low-impact action that meets every safe condition in the next section.
Make one change, observe the result and keep or reverse it.
Type fictional text in a new unsaved blank document.
The action may be legitimate, but it affects shared work, settings, software, permissions or something you are not authorised to decide alone.
Do not make the change. Ask Paul or the authorised person and explain exactly what the screen is requesting.
Change a setting in a work account or edit a shared file.
The action could create an immediate external, financial, privacy, data-loss or security consequence, or the request appears suspicious.
Do not continue, do not repeat the action and do not provide information. Record the message and report it.
Publish a live post, send a real email, purchase a subscription or allow an unknown app to access the device.

lesson.text: If more than one category seems possible

Use the more cautious category. Stop overrides Ask first, and Ask first overrides Safe to try. For example, installing approved work software normally means Ask first. Installing an unknown program from a suspicious message means Stop because the security risk is more serious.

lesson.label: Common mistake
lesson.text: Do not decide that an action is safe merely because the button is available or because the message looks professional. The effect of the action matters more than the appearance of the button.
2.3 Safe to try

A Safe to try action is a temporary, low-impact action that can be tested without affecting real work or other people. Use this category when learning a new feature in a controlled practice situation.
An action is Safe to try only when every condition below is true:
The information is fictional and has been provided for practice.
The action affects only your temporary personal practice, not a shared file, account or system.
The action does not delete, send, publish, purchase, upload real information or reduce security.
The action can be reversed or the temporary work can be closed without saving.
You understand what result should appear after the action.
You will make one change and then stop to observe the result.
Examples: typing a fictional sentence in an unsaved blank Word document; pressing Ctrl+Z once to remove the last fictional sentence you typed.
Common risk: treating a real document as practice. A copy of a real client file still contains real information and is not suitable for unrestricted practice.

The aim is not to make Rosie afraid of clicking anything. It is to help her pause long enough to notice the difference between harmless practice and an action that affects other people, shared information or the security of a device. Most everyday learning can continue safely when she uses fictional information and works in a file she created herself.

When unsure, Rosie should focus on the possible effect rather than the appearance of the button. A small button can still send, delete or publish something. A large menu can be harmless. Reading the wording carefully and asking what will change is more reliable than judging by how the screen looks.

lesson.label: Expected result
lesson.text: The practice change affects only the temporary document. You can see the result, reverse it if needed, and leave the real workplace information unchanged.

lesson.label: If the result is different
lesson.text: Stop making changes. Do not click repeatedly. Use Undo once only when the action was clearly a recent change in the temporary document. Otherwise record what happened and move to Ask first.
2.4 Ask first

Ask first means that the action may be normal workplace activity, but it requires approval, authority or context that you do not have. Asking first protects shared work and prevents an accidental change from affecting someone else.
Use Ask first when an action involves:
A shared file, shared folder, shared calendar, shared social media account or another person’s work.
A Windows, browser, email, application or account setting.
Installing, removing or updating software, add-ins, extensions or applications unless a specific approved process already authorises it.
A permission request, such as allowing an app to access files, the camera, the microphone, contacts or the device.
A request that may be legitimate but you are unsure whether you have authority to approve.
Any situation where the safe category is not clear.
Examples: correcting a spelling mistake in a file stored in a team folder; changing notification settings in the CV Made Better Gmail account.
Common risk: assuming a small change cannot matter. A small edit in a shared file can overwrite someone else’s work, change the approved version or create confusion about which copy is correct.

The aim is not to make Rosie afraid of clicking anything. It is to help her pause long enough to notice the difference between harmless practice and an action that affects other people, shared information or the security of a device. Most everyday learning can continue safely when she uses fictional information and works in a file she created herself.

When unsure, Rosie should focus on the possible effect rather than the appearance of the button. A small button can still send, delete or publish something. A large menu can be harmless. Reading the wording carefully and asking what will change is more reliable than judging by how the screen looks.

lesson.label: Exact method
lesson.text: Leave the item unchanged. Record what you were trying to do, the exact request or setting, what you expected and why approval is needed. Ask Paul or the authorised person before continuing.

lesson.label: Expected result
lesson.text: No shared or system change is made until approval and instructions are received.

lesson.label: If the result is different
lesson.text: If you already selected something and the screen changed unexpectedly, do not try several fixes. Stop, note the exact result and report it.
2.5 Stop

Stop means do not continue with the action now. It does not mean the action can never be completed. It means the possible consequence is serious enough that you must stop before any further click, entry or confirmation.
Use Stop when an action could:
Delete real or shared work, permanently remove information or empty a recycle bin.
Send, submit, publish, post or release something to a real person or public audience.
Purchase, pay, subscribe, start a trial or accept a charge.
Expose, upload, copy or share client information, personal information, passwords, access links or multi-factor authentication codes.
Turn off security, ignore a security warning, bypass protection or allow unknown remote access.
Open a suspicious link, download an unknown file or approve an unexpected access request.
Make an unexpected problem worse because the same action is being repeated.
Examples: selecting Publish on a live LinkedIn post; entering a client CV into a public tool that has not been approved for confidential information.
Common risk: trying to “finish quickly” because a warning interrupts the task. A warning is a reason to slow down, not a reason to bypass the control.

It is to help her pause long enough to notice the difference between harmless practice and an action that affects other people, shared information or the security of a device. lesson.label: Exact method
lesson.text: Take your hands away from the keyboard and mouse for a moment. Read the full message. Do not provide information, approve access or repeat the action. Record the exact wording and report it.

lesson.label: Expected result
lesson.text: The risky action is not completed and the possible harm is contained.

lesson.label: If the result is different
lesson.text: If the action has already happened, do not hide it or attempt several repairs. Report exactly what occurred and follow the incident instructions you are given.
2.6 What makes an action reversible

Reversible means that you can return to the previous state without losing needed information, affecting an outside person or relying on someone else to repair the result. Reversibility is a property of the whole action, not just the presence of an Undo button.
Use the reversibility test before trying an unfamiliar action:
1. What exactly will change?
2. Where will the change happen: a temporary practice item, a real file, a shared area, an account or the device?
3. Who else could see, receive or be affected by the change?
4. Can I return to the previous state now without losing information or asking another person to fix it?
5. Will anything leave the temporary practice document, such as an email, upload, post, payment or permission?
Reversible examples: removing the last fictional sentence with Undo; changing text in an unsaved temporary document and then closing it without saving.

Not reliably reversible examples: sending an email, publishing a post, purchasing a subscription, revealing information, permanently deleting a file or changing shared content that another person may already have used.

It is to help her pause long enough to notice the difference between harmless practice and an action that affects other people, shared information or the security of a device. lesson.label: Common mistake
lesson.text: An action is not automatically reversible because an Undo icon exists. Undo normally applies only inside the current application and only to certain recent changes.

lesson.label: If you cannot answer the reversibility test
lesson.text: Classify the action as Ask first. Uncertainty is a valid reason to request approval.
2.7 Fictional practice information

Fictional practice information is invented information that does not identify a real client, employee, family member or other person. It allows you to practise the method without creating a privacy or business consequence.
Fictional information matters because it:
Protects real client and personal information.
Allows mistakes to be corrected without affecting a real person.
Makes the task repeatable because everyone can use the same supplied details.
Makes it clear that the work is training rather than live workplace output.

Example 1: Northstar Career Services, Maya Patel, Operations Coordinator, maya.patel@example.com. Example 2: Greenfield Office Supplies, Daniel Brooks, Administration Assistant, daniel.brooks@example.com.

Common risk: changing only one detail in a real client record. The remaining information is still real. Do not use a real CV, real email address, real phone number, password, login, payment detail or private message for practice.

It is to help her pause long enough to notice the difference between harmless practice and an action that affects other people, shared information or the security of a device. Most everyday learning can continue safely when she uses fictional information and works in a file she created herself.

lesson.label: Exact method
lesson.text: Use only the fictional names, organisations, dates and text supplied in the workbook. When creating a temporary practice document, type FICTIONAL PRACTICE as the first line.

lesson.label: Expected result
lesson.text: The practice task can be completed, changed or discarded without exposing real information.
2.8 Shared files, settings, installed software and permissions

rows: A file that other people can open, edit or rely on.
Your change may overwrite, confuse or alter approved work.
A choice that changes how Windows, an app, browser or account behaves.
The effect may continue after the current task or reduce security.
A program, app, add-in or extension added to or changed on the device.
It can affect performance, access information or create licence and security risks.
Ask first, or Stop if unknown or suspicious
Approval that lets an app or person access a feature, file, account, camera, microphone or device.
The permission may expose information or allow changes.
Ask first, or Stop if unexpected or suspicious

lesson.text: When you ask for approval, describe the exact item. “Can I change a setting?” is less useful than “Gmail is asking whether I want to turn on automatic forwarding to an external address. I have not selected anything.”

A file is the individual item Rosie works on, such as a document or spreadsheet. A folder is the place used to group related files. A clear folder structure reduces the time spent searching and lowers the risk of editing the wrong version.

Good names should tell Rosie what the file contains without opening it. Dates, clear subjects and version words are useful when they follow one agreed pattern. Names such as ‘new’, ‘latest’ or ‘final final’ quickly become confusing because they do not explain the order of the files.
2.9 Actions with an outside or high-impact effect

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what actions with an outside or high-impact effect changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

rows: Information may be lost or difficult to recover.
Stop before deleting real or shared work.
The information leaves the draft and reaches another person or system.
Stop and check the recipient, content and approval.
The content becomes visible to an audience and may be copied.
Money, a contract or a recurring charge may be created.
Privacy, confidentiality or account access may be compromised.
Stop and do not enter or upload the information.
The device or account may become easier to access or infect.
Stop and do not bypass the warning or control.

lesson.text: 2.10 Make one change at a time
Making one change at a time means performing one deliberate action, pausing and checking the result before taking the next action. This makes cause and effect visible.
It matters because several quick changes can hide which action created the problem. One controlled change is easier to reverse, explain and repeat.
Example 1: press Ctrl+Z once, then check whether the last sentence disappeared. Example 2: select one menu option, observe the screen, then decide whether another step is needed.
Common risk: repeatedly clicking because the computer appears slow. The first click may still be processing, and extra clicks may open several windows or apply the action more than once.

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what make one change at a time changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.

lesson.label: Exact method
lesson.text: 1. Notice the starting point. 2. Make one change. 3. Pause and observe. 4. Compare the actual result with the expected result. 5. Keep, reverse or report the change before continuing.

lesson.label: Expected result
lesson.text: You can identify which action produced the visible change.

lesson.label: If the result is different
lesson.text: Do not add a second change. Record the difference and use the category rules.
2.11 Undo and Redo

Undo reverses the most recent change that the current application can still reverse. In Microsoft Word, you can use the left-curving Undo arrow near the top of the window or press Ctrl+Z. Ctrl+Z means hold the Ctrl key, press Z once and then release both keys.
Redo reapplies a change that was just undone. In Microsoft Word, use the right-curving Redo arrow or press Ctrl+Y. Ctrl+Y means hold the Ctrl key, press Y once and then release both keys.

rows: The most recent change disappears or returns to its previous state.
Reapplies the change that was just undone.

lesson.text: Use Undo and Redo one press at a time. After each press, look at the document. A second press affects an earlier action, not the same action again.
Examples: Undo removes the last sentence typed in a temporary document; Redo restores that sentence after it was undone.
Common risk: holding Ctrl+Z or pressing it many times without observing. This can reverse several earlier changes that you intended to keep.

Think of Undo as stepping back through recent changes, one step at a time. Redo moves forward again after an Undo. This is useful while drafting or practising, but it is not a safety net for every action. Closing a file, sending a message, deleting something permanently or changing an online account may not be recoverable in the same way.

A sensible habit is to pause after each change and look at the screen before continuing. If the result is wrong, Rosie can usually undo the most recent change while she still remembers exactly what she did. Making several changes quickly makes it harder to know which step caused the problem.

lesson.label: Expected result
lesson.text: One recent change is reversed or restored after one shortcut press.

lesson.label: If the result is different
lesson.text: Do not keep pressing the shortcut. Check whether the arrow is grey, whether the document was closed and reopened, or whether the action happened outside Word. Record the result and use Ask first.
2.12 Limits of Undo and Redo
Undo and Redo are useful recovery tools, but they are not a guarantee. Their history normally belongs to the current application and current open session.
Undo or Redo may not work when:
The document or application has been closed and reopened.
The application does not support reversing that particular action.
The action happened outside the current application, such as sending an email or publishing a post.
The action created a payment, permission, upload or security consequence.
The information was permanently deleted or another person has already used the changed shared information.
The application crashed or the undo history was cleared.
The Undo or Redo arrow is grey, which means the application has no available action of that type.
Common risk: relying on Undo as permission to try a high-impact action. The correct order is to classify the action first. Use Undo only after a Safe to try action or when specifically instructed.

lesson.label: What to do when Undo or Redo is unavailable
lesson.text: Stop. Do not repeatedly press the shortcut. If the work is a temporary fictional document and nothing needs to be kept, close it without saving. In any other situation, record the result and Ask first.
2.13 Describe an unexpected result accurately
An unexpected result is any screen, message or behaviour that is different from the result you were told to expect. Accurate descriptions help another person understand the problem without guessing.
A useful description contains five facts:

rows: What you were trying to complete.
I was practising Undo in a blank Word document.
The button, menu choice or shortcut used, including how many times.
What the lesson said should happen.
I expected the last sentence to disappear.
What changed, what did not change and the exact wording of any message.
The sentence stayed and the Undo arrow was grey.
What you did after noticing the difference.
I stopped and did not press the shortcut again.

lesson.text: Useful example: “In Microsoft Word, I pressed Ctrl+Y once after undoing a sentence. I expected the sentence to return. Nothing changed and the Redo arrow was grey. I stopped.”
Unhelpful example: “Word is broken.” This does not say what action was taken, what was expected or what appeared.
Common risk: paraphrasing a warning from memory. Record the exact wording while it is visible. Do not include passwords, full client information or security codes in the report.

The aim is not to make Rosie afraid of clicking anything. It is to help her pause long enough to notice the difference between harmless practice and an action that affects other people, shared information or the security of a device. Most everyday learning can continue safely when she uses fictional information and works in a file she created herself.

When unsure, Rosie should focus on the possible effect rather than the appearance of the button. A small button can still send, delete or publish something. A large menu can be harmless. Reading the wording carefully and asking what will change is more reliable than judging by how the screen looks.

lesson.label: If the result is different
lesson.text: The unexpected result is not a reason to experiment with several fixes. Stop, record the five facts and use Ask first or Stop according to the category rules.
2.14 The Safe Action Method

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what the safe action method changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.

rows: Have I stopped long enough to read the screen?
What exact words, button names or warning are visible?
What will change and who or what could be affected?
Is the whole action reversible without lost information or outside effect?
Is it Safe to try, Ask first or Stop?
What is the single approved next action?
If different, can I state the task, action, expectation, actual result and next safe step?

lesson.label: Lesson checkpoint
lesson.text: Before continuing, you should be able to explain the difference between Safe to try, Ask first and Stop; state what reversible means; explain why fictional information is used; describe Undo and Redo; and list the five facts in an unexpected result report.

worked_example.text: 3. Worked example

worked_example.label: Read this example first. Do not complete these steps yet.
worked_example.text: The example shows the complete reasoning process. You will perform a separate guided task afterwards.
Starting situation

Rosie is practising in Microsoft Word using a new blank document. She has typed the fictional heading “FICTIONAL PRACTICE”. A message appears: “QuickWriter Add-in wants permission to install and access your Word documents.” The message offers Allow and Cancel.
Objective
Decide safely, keep the device and information unchanged, then practise a reversible text change using Undo and Redo.
Part 1: Classify the permission request

rows: Rosie stops and does not select Allow.
This prevents an automatic response before the message is understood.
She reads the full message and notes the exact name “QuickWriter Add-in” and the request to install and access Word documents.
The exact wording identifies both installed software and a permission.
The request could change Word and give an add-in access to documents.
The effect is wider than the temporary practice text.
Rosie cannot be certain that installation and document access can be fully reversed without support.
An available Cancel button does not make selecting Allow safe.
She chooses Ask first. If the request came from a suspicious email or unknown download, she would use Stop.
Installed software and permissions require approval; suspicious access raises the category to Stop.
Cancel prevents the requested change. If no clear Cancel option existed, she would leave the message open and ask.
The message closes and the blank Word document remains visible.
This is the expected result because no add-in should be installed.
She writes: “Word displayed a QuickWriter Add-in permission request to install and access documents. I selected Cancel once. The message closed and the document remained unchanged.”
This gives exact, useful facts without exposing any real information.

worked_example.text: Part 2: Use Undo and Redo one change at a time
After the permission request has been cancelled, Rosie continues only with the temporary fictional document.
1. She types the sentence: Maya Patel is preparing for an operations role.
2. She types a second sentence: This sentence will be removed and restored.
3. She presses Ctrl+Z once and releases the keys. The second sentence disappears.
4. She pauses and observes. Because the expected result appeared, she continues.
5. She presses Ctrl+Y once and releases the keys. The second sentence returns.
6. She pauses again and observes before taking any other action.

Why these actions are Safe to try: the text is fictional, the document is temporary and unsaved, no information leaves the document, one recent change can be reversed and the expected result is known.

worked_example.label: Finished result
worked_example.text: The document displays the heading and both fictional sentences. The real device settings, shared files and workplace information remain unchanged.

worked_example.label: If the finished result were different
worked_example.text: Rosie would not press the shortcuts repeatedly. She would record the exact action, expected result, actual result and next safe step.
Part 3: Model unexpected result description
Suppose Ctrl+Y did not restore the sentence and the Redo arrow was grey. A useful report would be:

worked_example.label: Model report
worked_example.text:
Task: I was practising Redo in a blank Word document.
Exact action: I pressed Ctrl+Y once.
Expected result: I expected the sentence “This sentence will be removed and restored.” to return.
Actual result: Nothing changed and the Redo arrow was grey.
Next safe step: I stopped and did not press the shortcut again.

guided_practice.text: Guided Task 2: Practise Undo and Redo in Microsoft Word
Purpose: make a reversible text change, observe the result after each action and close the temporary document without saving.
What to open: Microsoft Word and a new blank document. You are creating a new temporary document. You are not using an existing file.

guided_practice.label: Before starting
guided_practice.text: Close or minimise unrelated work. Do not copy any client or personal information into the practice document. Use only the exact fictional text below.
Open the temporary document
1. Select the Windows Start button at the bottom of the screen.
2. Type Word.
3. Select Microsoft Word from the result. If Word is already open, select File, then New, then Blank document.
4. Select Blank document. You should see a white page with a flashing vertical line called the cursor.
5. If Word asks you to sign in, install something, enable a permission or change a setting, do not approve it. Use Ask first and record the exact message.
Enter the exact fictional text
1. Type: FICTIONAL PRACTICE
2. Press Enter once.
3. Type: Maya Patel is preparing for an operations role.
4. Press Enter once.
5. Type: This sentence will be removed and restored.

guided_practice.label: Expected result
guided_practice.text: The page shows three lines. The third line ends with a full stop.
Record what you can see before using Undo:
Use Undo and Redo one action at a time

rows: Hold Ctrl, press Z once, then release both keys.
Do not press again. Record the actual result below.
Hold Ctrl, press Y once, then release both keys.
Do not press again. Record the actual result below.
Press Ctrl+Z once. Pause. Then press Ctrl+Z once more.
After the first press, line 3 disappears. After the second press, line 2 disappears. The heading remains.
If more text disappears, stop and record how many times the shortcut was pressed.
If nothing changes, stop and record whether the Redo arrow is grey.

guided_practice.text: Close the temporary document
1. Select the X at the top-right of the Word window.
2. If Word asks whether to save the document, select Don’t Save. The document contains only fictional temporary practice and is not required later.
3. If a different message appears, do not guess. Leave the message visible and complete the Unexpected Result Report in Guided Task 3.
Guided Task 2 practical record

rows: Exact three lines were typed before shortcuts
Two separate Ctrl+Z presses removed lines 3 and 2 one at a time
The temporary document was closed without saving

guided_practice.text: Scoring: 2 points for each observable check. Maximum: 12 points.

lesson.text: 2. Complete lesson
Read this section before completing any activity.
2.1 The desktop, taskbar and Start menu

Definition: The desktop is the main Windows workspace. The taskbar is the strip, usually at the bottom, showing open and pinned applications. The Start menu is the main list and search area for applications.
Why it matters: Knowing these areas prevents random clicking and makes it easier to return to an application.
When to use it: Use them whenever opening, finding or switching applications.

Windows often keeps several programs open at once. The important skill is knowing which program is active and where the work has gone when a window is minimised or covered by another one. The taskbar acts like a row of doorways back into open programs.

Rosie does not need to close a program simply because she cannot see it. She should first check the taskbar, select the program and confirm whether the correct file is still open. This avoids reopening duplicate copies or losing track of where changes were made.
Examples: Selecting Start and typing Notepad; selecting the File Explorer folder icon on the taskbar.
Common mistake or risk: Confusing an application icon with a document file, or opening several copies of the same application.
Method:
1. Look at the taskbar before opening anything.
2. Select Start once.
3. Type the application name.
4. Select the matching application result.
5. Check the taskbar for its highlighted icon.
Expected result: The application opens and its taskbar icon appears active.
If the result is different: Press Esc to close the Start menu. If the wrong application opened, close it only if no work was entered, then repeat the search carefully.
2.2 Application windows
Definition: A window is the rectangular area in which an application or folder appears. Its title bar shows the application or file name.
Why it matters: The title bar and window controls help you identify what is open and avoid closing the wrong item.
When to use it: Use this whenever more than one application, folder or document is open.

Windows often keeps several programs open at once. The important skill is knowing which program is active and where the work has gone when a window is minimised or covered by another one. The taskbar acts like a row of doorways back into open programs.

Rosie does not need to close a program simply because she cannot see it. She should first check the taskbar, select the program and confirm whether the correct file is still open. This avoids reopening duplicate copies or losing track of where changes were made.
Examples: A Notepad window titled Untitled - Notepad; a File Explorer window titled Documents.
Common mistake or risk: Selecting Close when you intended to minimise, especially with unsaved work.
Method:
1. Read the title bar.
2. Locate Minimise, Maximise/Restore and Close at the top-right.
3. Choose only the control required.
4. Observe the taskbar and screen before taking another action.
Expected result: The window changes in the intended way while other work remains unchanged.
If the result is different: Use Module 1.1’s one-change-at-a-time rule. If a save prompt appears, stop and read it before choosing.
2.3 Minimise, maximise, restore and close
Definition: Minimise hides a window on the taskbar without closing it. Maximise fills the screen. Restore returns a maximised window to a movable size. Close ends the window or application.
Why it matters: These controls help organise the screen while protecting work.
When to use it: Minimise to temporarily hide; maximise for more space; restore to view two windows; close only when finished.

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what minimise, maximise, restore and close changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.
Examples: Minimise Notepad while checking a folder; restore File Explorer so Notepad can sit beside it.
Common mistake or risk: Assuming minimised means closed, or closing an unsaved document.
Method:
1. Confirm the window title.
2. Select the required control once.
3. Check the visible change.
4. To reopen a minimised window, select its taskbar icon.
Expected result: The window is hidden, enlarged, reduced or closed as selected.
If the result is different: If nothing changes, pause. Do not repeatedly click. Select the taskbar icon once or use Alt+Tab to check whether the window is behind another.
2.4 Switching between open applications
Definition: Switching means bringing a different open window to the front without closing the current one.
Why it matters: It supports tasks that use information from more than one application.
When to use it: Use taskbar icons or Alt+Tab when moving between open applications.

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what switching between open applications changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.
Examples: Switch from Notepad to File Explorer; use Alt+Tab to return to Notepad.
Common mistake or risk: Holding Alt+Tab too long and selecting the wrong preview.
Method:
1. Save current work if needed.
2. Select the required taskbar icon, or hold Alt and tap Tab once.
3. Release the keys when the correct preview is selected.
4. Read the title bar to confirm.
Expected result: The chosen window appears at the front and the other remains open.
If the result is different: Use the taskbar instead. Select each icon once until the correct title appears.
2.5 Moving and arranging windows
Definition: A restored window can be moved by dragging its title bar and resized from its edges. Windows can also snap side by side.
Why it matters: Arranging windows reduces repeated switching and makes comparison easier.
When to use it: Use it when reading from one window while entering information in another.

Windows often keeps several programs open at once. The important skill is knowing which program is active and where the work has gone when a window is minimised or covered by another one. The taskbar acts like a row of doorways back into open programs.

Rosie does not need to close a program simply because she cannot see it. She should first check the taskbar, select the program and confirm whether the correct file is still open. This avoids reopening duplicate copies or losing track of where changes were made.
Examples: Drag Notepad to the left and File Explorer to the right; resize a window by dragging its edge.
Common mistake or risk: Dragging from inside the document instead of the title bar, or making a window too narrow to read.
Method:
1. Restore the window if it is maximised.
2. Point to the title bar.
3. Hold the left mouse button and move the window.
4. Release when positioned.
5. Resize only from an edge or corner.
Expected result: Both windows remain visible and usable.
If the result is different: Maximise the window to recover a readable view, then restore and try again more slowly.

lesson.text: 2. Complete lesson
2.1 Files, folders and locations
Definition: A file stores information, such as a document or spreadsheet. A folder groups files. A location is the path showing where a file or folder is stored.
Why it matters: Clear locations prevent duplicate work and make files easier to retrieve.
When to use it: Use these ideas every time you create, save, move or search for work.

A file is the individual item Rosie works on, such as a document or spreadsheet. A folder is the place used to group related files. A clear folder structure reduces the time spent searching and lowers the risk of editing the wrong version.

Good names should tell Rosie what the file contains without opening it. Dates, clear subjects and version words are useful when they follow one agreed pattern. Names such as ‘new’, ‘latest’ or ‘final final’ quickly become confusing because they do not explain the order of the files.
Examples: A Word file stored in Documents > Rosie Training; a folder called Completed Work containing finished files.
Common mistake or risk: Treating the filename as the location, or saving the same file into several unrelated folders.
Method:
1. Before saving, identify the correct main folder.
2. Open or create the required subfolder.
3. Read the address bar to confirm the location.
4. Save once using the exact filename.
5. Check the file appears in that location.
Expected result: The file appears once in the intended folder and can be reopened.
If the result is different: Use File Explorer search for the exact filename. Do not create another copy until the original has been located or confirmed missing.
2.2 Professional folder structure
Definition: A folder structure is an organised hierarchy of main folders and subfolders.
Why it matters: A predictable structure helps anyone find current, reference and completed work.
When to use it: Use it for all workplace projects and recurring processes.

A file is the individual item Rosie works on, such as a document or spreadsheet. A folder is the place used to group related files. A clear folder structure reduces the time spent searching and lowers the risk of editing the wrong version.

Good names should tell Rosie what the file contains without opening it. Dates, clear subjects and version words are useful when they follow one agreed pattern. Names such as ‘new’, ‘latest’ or ‘final final’ quickly become confusing because they do not explain the order of the files.
Examples: Rosie Training > Volume 1 > Practice Files; Client Projects > Fictional Client > Drafts.
Common mistake or risk: Creating too many levels or vague folders such as Miscellaneous and New Folder.
Method:
1. Choose one clear main folder.
2. Create only the subfolders required by the process.
3. Use specific names describing content or stage.

2.1 The Word document area and insertion point
Definition: The document area is the page where content appears. The insertion point is the flashing vertical line showing where typed text will be placed.
Why it matters: Knowing where text will appear prevents accidental typing in the wrong position.
When to use it: Use it before typing, pasting or inserting a new paragraph.

Word separates the words Rosie writes from the way those words are presented. She can correct the content without redesigning the page, or adjust the layout without changing the meaning. Keeping those two jobs separate makes documents easier to review.

Before changing formatting, Rosie should select only the text that needs to change and notice what is currently selected. Many unexpected formatting problems happen because a whole paragraph, table or document was selected when only one word or heading was meant to change.
Examples: Click after a heading to continue it; click at the end of a paragraph before pressing Enter.
Common mistake or risk: Typing while text is selected, which replaces the selection.
Method:
1. Click once where text should begin.
2. Confirm the insertion point is visible.
3. Type a short amount.
4. Pause and check the result.
Expected result: Text appears at the insertion point without replacing other content.
If the result is different: Press Ctrl+Z once if the last typing replaced text, then click in the correct location and retry.
2.2 Selecting text
Definition: Selecting highlights text so the next command affects only that text.
Why it matters: Selection is essential for controlled formatting and editing.
When to use it: Use it before applying bold, changing size, copying or deleting specific text.

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what selecting text changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.
Examples: Drag across a heading; double-click a word.
Common mistake or risk: Leaving extra punctuation or spaces outside the selection, or accidentally selecting too much.
Method:
1. Place the pointer at the start.
2. Hold the left mouse button and drag to the end.
3. Release and check the highlighted text.
4. Apply one command.
5. Click once to remove the selection.
Expected result: Only the intended text changes.
If the result is different: Undo once, then repeat the selection more carefully. Use Shift plus arrow keys for small adjustments.
2.3 Paragraphs and line breaks
Definition: Pressing Enter creates a new paragraph. A paragraph carries formatting such as alignment and spacing.
Why it matters: Separate paragraphs improve readability and allow consistent formatting.
When to use it: Use a new paragraph for headings, separate ideas and list items.

2.1 Reviewing content before appearance
Definition: Content review checks whether words, facts, quantities and meaning are correct before focusing on visual consistency.
Why it matters: A polished layout cannot repair incorrect information.
When to use it: Use it after drafting and before final formatting.

Word separates the words Rosie writes from the way those words are presented. She can correct the content without redesigning the page, or adjust the layout without changing the meaning. Keeping those two jobs separate makes documents easier to review.

Before changing formatting, Rosie should select only the text that needs to change and notice what is currently selected. Many unexpected formatting problems happen because a whole paragraph, table or document was selected when only one word or heading was meant to change.
Examples: Check a date against supplied source material; confirm a list contains exactly three required items.
Common mistake or risk: Reading for spelling only and missing an incorrect date or omitted instruction.
Method:
1. Read the task or source material first.
2. Check names, dates, numbers and required points.
3. Read each sentence for meaning.
4. Mark only confirmed changes.
5. Recheck quantities after editing.
Expected result: The document communicates the supplied information accurately and completely.
If the result is different: Stop and compare with the supplied source. Do not invent missing facts.
2.2 Spelling and grammar suggestions
Definition: Word may underline text and offer suggestions. A suggestion is a possible change, not an instruction.
Why it matters: Automated checking catches some errors but can misunderstand names, context and UK English.
When to use it: Use it after content review, one suggestion at a time.

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what spelling and grammar suggestions changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.
Examples: Correct recieve to receive; ignore a fictional organisation name that Word does not recognise.
Common mistake or risk: Accepting every suggestion automatically or changing meaning to satisfy the checker.
Method:
1. Select an underlined word or open Editor.
2. Read the full sentence.
3. Compare the suggestion with the intended meaning and UK English.
4. Accept only a clearly correct suggestion.
5. Ignore or add to dictionary only when authorised and certain.
Expected result: Confirmed errors are corrected without changing correct names or meaning.
If the result is different: Undo the accepted suggestion and restore the intended wording. Record uncertain items for review.
2.3 Find and Replace
Definition: Find locates repeated text. Replace changes matching text. Replace All changes every match and therefore needs caution.
Why it matters: It can correct repeated errors consistently but may also alter unintended text.
When to use it: Use Find to review occurrences; use Replace one occurrence at a time when context matters.

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what find and replace changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.
Examples: Find every use of organise; replace a fictional date after checking each occurrence.
Common mistake or risk: Using Replace All before checking how the word appears in different contexts.
Method:
1. Save the document first.
2. Press Ctrl+H for Replace.
3. Enter the exact text to find and replacement text.
4. Choose Find Next.
5. Read the surrounding sentence.
6. Select Replace for each confirmed occurrence.
Expected result: Only intended occurrences change.

If the result is different: Press Ctrl+Z immediately if the last replacement was wrong. If Replace All caused widespread changes, close without saving only if no other unsaved work would be lost; otherwise restore from a known version.
2.4 Track changes versus direct editing
Definition: Direct editing changes the document immediately. Track Changes records insertions and deletions for review.
Why it matters: The correct method depends on whether a reviewer must see edits.
When to use it: Use direct editing for your own controlled practice; use Track Changes only when the workflow requires review and it has been taught or approved.

Word separates the words Rosie writes from the way those words are presented. She can correct the content without redesigning the page, or adjust the layout without changing the meaning. Keeping those two jobs separate makes documents easier to review.

Examples: Correct a typo directly in a practice file; use tracked changes in an authorised client review workflow.
Common mistake or risk: Turning Track Changes on accidentally and delivering a document with unresolved marks.
Method:
1. Check whether review marks are required.
2. For this module, keep Track Changes off.
3. Make one direct edit.
4. Save and inspect the final view.
Expected result: The document shows clean final text with no review marks.
If the result is different: Open the Review tab and check Track Changes status. Do not accept or reject another person’s changes without approval.
2.5 Final visual and file checks
Definition: Final checks confirm consistent headings, spacing, bullets, page breaks, filename and save location.
Why it matters: They prevent professional errors after the wording is correct.
When to use it: Use immediately before marking a document complete.

A file is the individual item Rosie works on, such as a document or spreadsheet. A folder is the place used to group related files. A clear folder structure reduces the time spent searching and lowers the risk of editing the wrong version.

4. Save the final version with the required filename.
5. Close and reopen it.
Expected result: The final file is clean, complete, consistently formatted and retrievable.
If the result is different: Return to the exact issue, correct one item, save and reopen again.

2.1 What a formula is
Definition: A formula is an instruction in a cell that begins with = and calculates a result from values or cell references.

Common mistake or risk: Typing a result manually or omitting the equals sign, which leaves text instead of a calculation.
Method:
1. Select the result cell.
2. Type = followed by the function and range.
3. Press Enter.
4. Select the cell and check the formula bar.
5. Compare the result with an independent check.
Expected result: The cell displays a numeric result and the formula bar shows the formula.
If the result is different: Check the equals sign, function spelling, brackets and range. Use Undo if the wrong cell was changed.

Why it matters: Correct references ensure the formula uses the intended data.

2.3 SUM and AVERAGE

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.
Examples: Official product support page updated in 2026; reputable industry guide citing official documentation.
Common mistake or risk: Relying on an undated blog, copied list or search snippet when an official source exists.
Method:
1. Identify publisher and purpose.
2. Check the page directly answers the question.
3. Find publication or update date where available.
4. Locate the exact supporting statement.
5. Compare with a second credible source for important claims.
Expected result: The source has a clear reason to be trusted and directly supports the recorded fact.
If the result is different: Mark the point unverified. Search for an official or independent confirming source rather than filling the gap.
2.4 Fact, interpretation and assumption
Definition: A fact is directly supported by evidence. An interpretation explains what the fact may mean. An assumption fills a gap without evidence.
Why it matters: Separating them prevents confident but unsupported workplace advice.
When to use it: Use it when writing research notes or recommendations.

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what fact, interpretation and assumption changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.
Examples: Fact: the supplied guide states 1600 × 900 pixels. Interpretation: this should provide a wide landscape image. Assumption: every platform accepts the same size.
Common mistake or risk: Presenting an interpretation or assumption as a confirmed fact.
Method:
1. Write the source-supported statement.
2. Label any explanation as interpretation.
3. Identify missing information.
4. Do not convert missing information into a claim.
5. State what must be verified next.
Expected result: Readers can distinguish confirmed information from judgement and gaps.
If the result is different: Rewrite the note with explicit labels and remove unsupported certainty.
2.5 Recording sources
Definition: A research record captures the question, search terms, source title, publisher, date, link, evidence and conclusion.
Why it matters: It allows another person to verify the work and reduces repeated searching.
When to use it: Use for any research that affects published content, client advice or business decisions.

Finding a webpage is only the first part of research. Rosie also needs to decide who published it, when it was updated and whether it actually supports the point she wants to use. A polished website can still contain old, incomplete or promotional information.

For an important fact, Rosie should compare more than one dependable source and open the pages rather than relying on the short wording shown in search results. If the sources disagree, she should record the difference instead of choosing the answer she prefers.
Examples: Record an official support article title and exact URL; note no date was visible.
Common mistake or risk: Saving only a link with no explanation or copying long passages without identifying the relevant point.
Method:
1. Create one row per source.
2. Record full title and publisher.
3. Record publication or access date.
4. Summarise the supporting evidence in your own words.
5. State whether the source is accepted, supporting or rejected.
Expected result: The final conclusion can be traced to evidence.
If the result is different: Reopen the source and complete missing fields. If the page cannot be accessed, mark it unavailable and seek another source.

lesson.text: 2. Complete lesson
2.1 Troubleshooting is controlled observation
Definition: Troubleshooting is the process of identifying what happened, checking likely causes and testing one safe change at a time.
Why it matters: A controlled process prevents panic, repeated actions and accidental damage.
When to use it: Use it when software, files, windows or internet behaviour differs from the expected result.

Troubleshooting works best as a calm process of narrowing down the cause. Rosie should first describe what she expected, what actually happened and what changed immediately beforehand. This is more useful than saying that the computer ‘is broken’.

The safest approach is to try one low-risk step, check the result and then decide what to do next. Trying several fixes together may hide the cause or create a second problem. If an action needs a password, installation, permission change or security setting, Rosie should stop and ask first.
Examples: A file does not appear in the expected folder; an application window is hidden behind another.
Common mistake or risk: Clicking repeatedly, changing several settings or restarting without recording what happened.
Method:
1. Stop repeating the failed action.
2. State the expected result.
3. State the actual result.
4. Record the last action completed.
5. Classify the next action as Safe to try, Ask first or Stop.
6. Test one safe change and observe.
Expected result: The problem becomes more specific and the effect of each test is known.
If the result is different: Return to the last known state, undo the safe test if possible and report the exact observations.
2.2 Check the simple visible causes first
Definition: Simple visible causes include the wrong window, wrong folder, misspelt filename, hidden application or incomplete entry.
Why it matters: Many everyday problems are navigation or location issues rather than system failures.
When to use it: Use before changing settings, reinstalling software or asking someone to repair the device.

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what check the simple visible causes first changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.
Examples: Check the title bar; check the File Explorer address bar.
Common mistake or risk: Assuming the computer lost a file when it was saved in another folder.
Method:
1. Read the active window title.
2. Check the taskbar for hidden windows.
3. Check the folder path or browser address.
4. Check spelling and required values.
5. Repeat only the intended step once.
Expected result: The cause is identified or ruled out without changing system settings.
If the result is different: Record that the visible checks passed and move to the next taught check.
2.3 Safe first responses

Definition: Safe first responses are low-impact actions such as waiting briefly, switching windows, reopening a saved file, using Undo or closing and reopening a non-critical application after saving.
Why it matters: They often restore normal operation without affecting settings or data.
When to use it: Use only when the action meets Module 1.1 Safe to try conditions.

This idea becomes easier when Rosie connects it to a real piece of work rather than trying to memorise a definition. The important question is what safe first responses changes, who or what may be affected, and how she can check that the result is sensible.

Rosie should work slowly enough to notice the result of each step. When something looks different from the lesson, she should stop, describe the difference and return to the last confirmed step instead of guessing what to press next.
Examples: Use Alt+Tab to find a hidden window; reopen a verified saved document.
Common mistake or risk: Closing an application with unsaved work or restarting the computer during an update.
Method:
1. Save current work if possible.
2. Choose one reversible response.
3. Perform it once.
4. Wait for the result.
5. Compare actual and expected behaviour.
Expected result: The issue is resolved or one possible cause is eliminated.
If the result is different: Undo or reverse the test where possible. Stop if a warning, permission request, security issue or risk to real data appears.
2.4 When to ask first or stop

Definition: Ask first applies to settings, shared files, software, permissions and unclear authority. Stop applies to security warnings, suspicious messages, deletion, publishing, payment, exposure or worsening behaviour.
Why it matters: Escalation protects workplace systems and information.
When to use it: Use whenever the next proposed action is not clearly low impact and reversible.

The aim is not to make Rosie afraid of clicking anything. It is to help her pause long enough to notice the difference between harmless practice and an action that affects other people, shared information or the security of a device. Most everyday learning can continue safely when she uses fictional information and works in a file she created herself.

When unsure, Rosie should focus on the possible effect rather than the appearance of the button. A small button can still send, delete or publish something. A large menu can be harmless. Reading the wording carefully and asking what will change is more reliable than judging by how the screen looks.
Examples: Ask before changing browser settings; stop when an unexpected remote-access request appears.
Common mistake or risk: Treating escalation as failure and continuing alone to appear confident.
Method:
1. Classify the next action.
2. For Ask first, pause and report what approval is needed.
3. For Stop, do not continue and preserve evidence such as the exact message.
4. Do not send passwords or codes.
5. Wait for authorised instructions.
Expected result: The issue is contained and the person helping receives useful information.
If the result is different: If an unsafe action was already taken, report it immediately and state exactly what was selected or entered.
2.5 A useful problem report
Definition: A problem report states context, expected result, actual result, exact message, last successful step, actions already tried and current status.
Why it matters: Specific reports reduce guesswork and repeated questions.
When to use it: Use when asking Paul, support or an authorised colleague for help.

Troubleshooting works best as a calm process of narrowing down the cause. Rosie should first describe what she expected, what actually happened and what changed immediately beforehand. This is more useful than saying that the computer ‘is broken’.

The safest approach is to try one low-risk step, check the result and then decide what to do next. Trying several fixes together may hide the cause or create a second problem. If an action needs a password, installation, permission change or security setting, Rosie should stop and ask first.
Examples: Expected file in Practice Files; actual file not visible; searched exact name; no error message.
Common mistake or risk: Writing “it does not work” without naming the application, file or result.
Method:
1. Name the application, file and location.
2. State what you expected.
3. State what actually happened.
4. Copy the exact error text if present.
5. State the last successful step.
6. List each safe action tried once.
7. State whether work is saved and whether the issue is continuing.
Expected result: Another person can understand and reproduce the problem without guessing.
If the result is different: Add the missing field. Do not interpret an error message when you can copy it exactly.
